title: Diagnostic Burden in Clinical Care: A Critical Review of Meanings and Measurement Boundaries
content: Background and Objectives: Diagnostic burden appears in research on screening, clinical evaluation and follow-up. Its interpretation depends on whose burden is considered and how it is measured. This review examines selected uses and proposes a qualified description of the patient-experienced diagnostic facet of wider healthcare burden. Materials and Methods: An exact-phrase search using PubMed's Title/Abstract field with a publication-date upper bound of 5 November 2026 provided a discovery inventory of 104 records. Twelve complete, publicly retrievable full texts were selected purposively for contextual examination. OpenAlex searches and targeted retrieval identified adjacent conceptual frameworks. Extraction assisted by artificial intelligence (AI) compared the bearer, diagnostic purpose and phase, operational definition, measure and supported inference. Results: Selected uses concerned procedure counts, healthcare contacts, professional tasks, program testing requirements and reported patient experiences. A published multicancer-screening model already explicitly defines diagnostic burden as procedures required for diagnostic resolution. Patient-centred imaging recommendations and treatment-burden frameworks already describe much of the relevant patient work and impact. The proposed definition concerns work a person experiences as demanding and adverse effects attributable to evaluation intended to detect, explain, confirm, exclude or characterize a health condition or finding. A reporting specification links each burden claim to its stakeholder and analytic unit, diagnostic purpose and phase, observed measure, comparison and inference. Conclusion: Context-dependent uses can be appropriate to their original purpose. Cross-study interpretation requires attention to measured diagnostic activity, resource demands and experienced impact. The proposed patient-focused definition and reporting specification require stakeholder appraisal and empirical testing.
